questions.explain: pwd stands for "print working directory" — it tells you exactly where you currently are in the filesystem.

questions.q: What distinguishes an absolute path from a relative path?
options: An absolute path starts from / and is valid from anywhere; a relative path is interpreted from your current location
A relative path always starts with a tilde
An absolute path only works inside /home
questions.explain: An absolute path begins at the root (/) and works no matter where you currently are. A relative path is interpreted relative to your current working directory.

questions.q: After running `cd /var/log`, what does `cd ..` do next?
options: Returns you to your home directory
Moves you up to /var, the parent of /var/log
questions.explain: `..` refers to the parent of the current directory, so from /var/log it moves you to /var.

questions.q: Why does a plain `ls` sometimes seem to be missing files like `.bashrc`?
options: Plain ls hides files starting with a dot; the -a flag is needed to show them
Dotfiles are a Windows-only concept and don't exist on Linux
questions.explain: ls hides "hidden" files — those whose names start with a dot — unless you pass -a, which shows all entries including dotfiles.

options: Takes you to your home directory
Jumps back to the directory you were in before your last cd command
questions.explain: cd - switches you back to whichever directory you were in immediately before your most recent cd, useful for bouncing between two locations.
